title: Lipase and amylase
subtitle: Pancreatitis interpretation and important alternative causes
summary: Pancreatitis interpretation and important alternative causes
introduction: Acute pancreatitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by characteristic pain and pancreatic enzyme elevation or imaging. Raised lipase/amylase alone is not diagnostic.

rows.name: Lipase
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult reference: 13–60 U/L; retain the ≥3 × upper-limit clinical pancreatitis threshold separately
notes: Lipase is generally more pancreas-specific and remains raised longer than amylase. It may also rise with renal failure, bowel ischaemia/obstruction, cholecystitis, perforation, DKA or medications.

rows.name: Amylase
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult reference: 28–100 U/L; retain the ≥3 × upper-limit clinical pancreatitis threshold separately
notes: Can be normal in delayed presentation, hypertriglyceridaemia or chronic pancreatic disease. Salivary disease, renal failure, bowel pathology and macroamylasaemia can also raise it.

urgentFindings: Severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension or fever.
Jaundice, fever and right-upper-quadrant pain suggesting biliary obstruction/cholangitis.
Peritonism (rigidity, involuntary guarding or rebound), shock, GI bleeding or reduced consciousness.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Likely acute pancreatitis picture
findings: Lipase (or amylase) ≥3 × the upper limit of normal
Severe, persistent epigastric pain, often radiating to the back
interpretation: This combination is consistent with acute pancreatitis, but the diagnosis remains clinical — enzyme elevation supports rather than confirms it, and severity is not predicted by the enzyme level
Common causes include gallstones and alcohol; also consider hypertriglyceridaemia, medication and, rarely, ERCP-related or autoimmune causes
actions: Assess severity using local scoring/physiology (tachycardia, hypotension, fever, oxygenation) rather than the enzyme level alone
Treat as time-critical if there is shock, peritonism, GI bleeding or reduced consciousness (see urgent findings)
Request further testing to identify the cause and assess severity (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Raised lipase with normal/borderline amylase
findings: Amylase normal or only mildly raised
Presentation more than 24–48 hours after symptom onset, or chronic pancreatic disease
interpretation: Amylase can normalise faster than lipase and can be falsely reassuring in delayed presentation, hypertriglyceridaemia or chronic pancreatic disease — lipase is generally the more reliable and pancreas-specific test
A normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis when lipase is raised and the clinical picture fits
actions: Do not use a normal amylase alone to exclude pancreatitis if lipase is raised and the history fits
Ask about symptom duration, alcohol use and known triglyceride/lipid problems
Arrange medical review for further assessment, including imaging if the diagnosis remains unclear (see further testing)

commonPatterns.title: Mild rise — consider a non-pancreatic cause
findings: Lipase and/or amylase raised but below the ≥3× pancreatitis threshold
Renal impairment, bowel obstruction/ischaemia, cholecystitis, perforation, DKA, salivary disease or relevant medication
interpretation: Mild-to-moderate elevation is non-specific and can arise from several non-pancreatic sources; renal failure alone can raise both enzymes through reduced clearance
Macroamylasaemia is a benign cause of isolated raised amylase without pancreatic disease, though it cannot be distinguished from other causes by this test alone
actions: Correlate with renal function, abdominal examination and the wider clinical picture rather than treating a mild rise as pancreatitis
Request U&E and consider capillary glucose/ketones if DKA is a differential (see further testing)
Arrange medical review to investigate the alternative cause suggested by the clinical picture

commonPatterns.title: Biliary obstruction with possible pancreatitis overlap
interpretation: Gallstone disease can cause both biliary obstruction/cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis together; this combination needs urgent assessment as ascending cholangitis is time-critical in its own right
actions: Treat as time-critical if jaundice, fever and right-upper-quadrant pain suggest cholangitis (see urgent findings)
Request liver blood tests and FBC/CRP to characterise the biliary and inflammatory picture (see further testing)
Arrange urgent hospital assessment for imaging and biliary intervention as well as pancreatitis management

rationale: Assesses renal function (a non-pancreatic cause of enzyme elevation) and hydration status, which are important for fluid resuscitation planning in pancreatitis
Deranged liver blood tests support a gallstone/biliary cause of pancreatitis and help identify co-existing biliary obstruction or cholangitis

furtherTesting.test: Full blood count and C-reactive protein
rationale: Support assessment of the inflammatory response and are used alongside physiology in severity assessment of pancreatitis
Hypercalcaemia is a recognised cause of pancreatitis, and hypocalcaemia can occur as a complication of severe pancreatitis
DKA can raise lipase/amylase and can also coexist with or mimic an acute abdomen, so should be considered when the picture is unclear
Needed to identify gallstones as a cause, assess complications, and support the diagnosis when the biochemical picture is equivocal

specimens.notes: Plasma — green-top lithium-heparin tube with yellow insert, 3 mL.
